title: Tumours as dynamical systems
summary: Exponential and Gompertz growth, what “detectable” means in cell counts, and two competing theories of how chemotherapy kills — tested in a lab.

shots.title:
Tumours as
dynamical systems.
shots.subtitle: Two growth laws, two theories of treatment.
shots.narration: Mathematical oncology starts with an ordinary differential equation for the number of cells. It is the friendliest entry point for a physicist — and a lesson in how much a model's assumptions decide its advice.

notes: Gompertz: growth slows towards a plateau K
Gompertz wrote it down in 1825 — for human mortality
shots.narration: Two classical laws. Exponential growth doubles every T d. Gompertz growth slows as the tumour approaches a plateau K; its relative growth rate decays exponentially. Gompertz first wrote it down in 1825, to describe human mortality.

shots.xLabel: Years from the first cancer cell
shots.narration: With a sixty-day doubling time, an exponential tumour reaches a billion cells in about five years. A Gompertz tumour with the same starting speed takes about nine. Either way, it was growing silently for years.

shots.label: doublings from one cell to about 10⁹ cells — roughly one gram
shots.narration: From one cell, thirty doublings make about a billion cells — roughly a gram. Ten more make a trillion. So by the time a tumour is detectable, most of its doublings are already behind it.

shots.text: “10⁹ cells per gram” is a **convention**. For epithelial tumours, **10⁸** may be closer.
shots.narration: Be careful with that conversion: a billion cells per gram is a convention, and one analysis argues that for epithelial tumours a hundred million is more realistic. Factors of ten hide in oncology's round numbers.

shots.text: Fitting is easy; **forecasting** is hard. In mice, no growth model forecast lung tumours beyond the next measurement without prior information.
shots.narration: In mouse experiments, Gompertz described breast-tumour growth best. But for lung tumours, no model forecast beyond the next measurement reliably, unless prior information on the parameters was added.

left.heading: Log-kill (Skipper)
items: Each dose kills a fixed fraction
Same number of logs whatever the size

shots.narration: Two theories of how chemotherapy kills. Log-kill says each dose removes a fixed fraction of cells, whatever the tumour's size. Norton and Simon say kill tracks the growth rate — so large, slow tumours barely respond.

shots.text: Under log-kill, curing a detectable tumour needs about **nine logs of net kill** — after regrowth between doses.
shots.narration: Under log-kill, curing a just-detectable tumour of a billion cells means about nine logs of net kill — that is, after subtracting regrowth between doses.

shots.text: Your lab: grow a tumour from one cell, then try to cure it — **under both theories**.
shots.narration: Now the lab. Grow a tumour from one cell, design a schedule that cures it under log-kill, then switch to Norton–Simon and see whether your schedule survives a change of theory.

steps.title: Lab: grow and treat a tumour
steps.brief: A teaching model: one cell population, no resistance, no toxicity limit. Use it to build intuition about logs, doublings and schedules — not to predict any patient.

steps.title: Notebook: tumour growth
steps.brief: Save your run in the lab, then interpret it.

fields.label: Which schedule cured the tumour under log-kill, and did it survive Norton–Simon? Why?
Name two things the model ignores (e.g. resistant clones, toxicity, drug delivery) and how each would change your conclusion.

questions.prompt: Exponential growth, doubling time 60 days. How many days from one cell to 2³⁰ cells?
How many logs (base 10) does a dose that kills 99.9% of cells remove?
questions.explain: Surviving fraction 10⁻³ → three logs. Under log-kill it removes three logs whatever the tumour's size.

questions.prompt: A tumour of 10⁹ cells gets 6 doses of 2 logs each, with no regrowth. What is log₁₀ of the cells left?
questions.explain: 9 − 6 × 2 = −3: on average 0.001 cells, which in the model means cure. With regrowth between doses you need more.

questions.prompt: Under Norton–Simon, which tumour loses the most logs per dose?
options: A large tumour near its plateau
questions.explain: Kill tracks the relative growth rate, which is highest when the tumour is small.

fields.label: 1. Solve dN/dt = b·N·ln(K/N) with N(0) = N₀. (Hint: substitute u = ln(N/K).) Show it gives the Gompertz curve above, and find its relative growth rate as a function of N.
2. With three noisy measurements early in growth, why can't you tell exponential from Gompertz? Relate your answer to the mouse forecasting study and say what extra information would help.
3. Is there any role for a quantum computer in tumour-growth modelling? Give your honest answer and the strongest counter-argument.
